findings.text: Within the first paragraph a newcomer can say what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves. This is the page's main strength.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The lede sells Athena as a tool that turns a request into a commit, but the rest of the page shows a different ability: reading another project. A newcomer may not see how the study relates to the product's main job. No example of a request turning into a traced commit is shown.
findings.source: "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it"

findings.text: Apart from three short lede paragraphs and Next steps, the page covers firstmate's internals: 12 transition cards and 45 claims. Someone who came to learn about Athena has to scroll past all of it, or use the early 'Next step' link, to find out how to try Athena.
findings.source: Page title "Athena explains how firstmate handles work" and the sections States, Counters, Transitions, Claims and sources

findings.text: The next step is easy to find and concrete: clone the repo, list of prerequisites, ./setup.sh, then an example command, athena ask "add a changelog". This gives a newcomer a clear path forward.
findings.source: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" and the Next steps section

findings.text: This link sits in the header, but the page never says who the 'owner' is or what the proposals are. For a first-time visitor it is unexplained.
findings.source: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: The list promises to define the words used in the text that follows, but 'place' first appears in "If every place of a declared capacity is held, the spawn exits 75" and is defined only in the Glossary. 'PR' and 'exit 75' are also used before they are explained.
findings.source: Words used first: "These words appear in the sentences that follow. Each is defined here"

findings.text: The page has no 'concurrency entry'. The only card about concurrency is ra3, and it cites c5 and c6, not the secondmate claims. A reader following this pointer finds nothing.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f2: "The page attaches those claims to the counter, to the relaunch transition, to the queued state and to the concurrency entry."

findings.text: The page is honest about this gap, but it leaves the key condition of the yolo merge rule undefined. A reader still cannot tell when firstmate will merge on its own.
findings.source: in scope: "The cited instruction does not say what makes work in scope, so this page gives no test for it."

findings.text: The list says t9 (ready → reopened) changes the place counter, but the t9 card never mentions places. A reader cannot tell from the card how t9 affects the count.
findings.source: Counters: "places-held, changed by transitions t1, t3, t4, t9, t11"

findings.text: The page states openly that nothing was run and links every claim to exact source lines at a pinned commit. A sceptical reader can check any statement for themselves.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f1: "no failure or retry edge was observed; every claim is marked read"

findings.text: Several definitions appear twice, word for word, and the cards repeat the same rules again (for example, red PRs are never merged). The repetition makes an already dense page longer for a first-time reader.
findings.source: Definitions of yolo, green, red and in scope under "Words used first" and again under "Glossary"
